title: fix(docker): standalone bundle omits @wreq-js native binding, breaking Codex app-server WebSocket

body:
### OmniRoute Version

3.8.51

### Installation Method

Docker / Docker Compose

### Operating System

Linux

### OS Version

Debian 13 with Dokploy

### Node.js Version

_No response_

### Provider(s) Involved

Codex App Server

### Model(s) Involved

cxa/gpt-5.6-luna -> codex-app-server/gpt-5.6-luna

### Client Tool

Codex CLI

### Description

Connecting a containerized `codex-app-server` to OmniRoute via WebSocket fails immediately with `Codex app-server websocket transport unavailable.`
The root cause is that wreq-js fails to load inside the Next.js standalone Docker runtime `([TlsClient] wreq-js unavailable; TLS fingerprint transport disabled)`. The dynamic `createRequire(import.meta.url)` in `open-sse/utils/tlsClient.ts` throws an error inside the compiled .next/standalone environment, swallowing the exception and hard-nulling `this.websocketFn`.
This module resolution failure persists even if the native `@wreq-js/binding-linux-x64-gnu` binary is manually injected into the container with correct node user permissions, pre-loaded via `NODE_OPTIONS=--require`, or entirely polyfilled with the standard ws library. The Next.js standalone tracer seems to aggressively isolate or mangle the dynamic require path, very similar to the tsx issue described in #12152 .

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy `diegosouzapw/omniroute:next` (or v3.8.50) via Docker Compose.
2. Deploy a secondary `ghcr.io/icoretech/codex-docker:latest` container exposing port 1456.
3. Configure OmniRoute with `OMNIROUTE_CODEX_APPSERVER_WS=ws://codex-app-server:1456` and the associated token file.
4. Start the stack and observe the immediate `[TlsClient] wreq-js unavailable warning` in the OmniRoute logs.
5. Send a chat completion request to a Codex App Server model (e.g., cxa/gpt-5.6-luna).
6. The request instantly fails with a 502 WebSocket transport unavailable error.

### Expected Behavior

OmniRoute successfully loads the WebSocket transport and establishes a JSON-RPC connection to the local app-server. Alternatively, since the local app-server explicitly ignores TLS fingerprinting (as noted in `appServerClient.ts`), it should safely fall back to the native Node `ws` library rather than strictly requiring `wreq-js`.

### Actual Behavior

Next.js fails to resolve `wreq-js` dynamically, disabling the WebSocket factory globally. Routing requests to the app-server instantly throws: `[STREAM] CODEX-APP-SERVER | gpt-5.6-luna | 88ms | error: Codex app-server websocket transport unavailable`.

### Test Impact

Needs a new integration test

### Error Logs / Output

```shell
▲ Next.js 16.3.2
- Local:         http://localhost:20128
- Network:       http://0.0.0.0:20128
✓ Ready in 0ms
✓ Running next.config took 3ms
[TlsClient] wreq-js unavailable; TLS fingerprint transport disabled
...
{"level":30,"time":"2026-09-01T18:50:59.743Z","service":"omniroute","module":"sse","tag":"HTTP","method":"POST","path":"/v1/chat/completions | cxa/gpt-5.6-luna | 1 msgs","msg":"📥 POST /v1/chat/completions | cxa/gpt-5.6-luna | 1 msgs"}
{"level":30,"time":"2026-09-01T18:50:59.797Z","service":"omniroute","module":"sse","tag":"ROUTING","msg":"cxa/gpt-5.6-luna → codex-app-server/gpt-5.6-luna"}
{"level":30,"time":"2026-09-01T18:50:59.812Z","service":"omniroute","module":"sse","tag":"AUTH","msg":"Using codex-app-server account: ***..."}
[18:50:59] 🌊 [STREAM] CODEX-APP-SERVER | gpt-5.6-luna | 88ms | error: Codex app-server websocket transport unavailable
{"level":40,"time":"2026-09-01T18:51:00.024Z","service":"omniroute","module":"sse","tag":"AUTH","msg":"[T-PROBE] noauth codex-app-server failure 502 recorded — connection stays in the pool"}
```

### Screenshots

_No response_

### Additional Context

Troubleshooting confirmed the native `wreq-js` binding works flawlessly at the OS/Node level inside the container (`node -e "console.log(require('wreq-js'))"` succeeds when mounted with correct UID 1000 ownership). The failure is strictly isolated to Next.js's standalone execution context swallowing the dynamic require. Since `wreq-js` is an optional dependency, it likely needs to be explicitly added to `EXTRA_MODULE_ENTRIES` or `experimental.serverComponentsExternalPackages` in the Next.js build pipeline so the tracer preserves it.

title: feat(docker): pin exact versions of the four AI CLIs in the runner-cli stage

labels.name: dependencies
labels.description: Pull requests that update a dependency file

labels.name: docker
labels.description: Pull requests that update docker code

body:
## Summary
The `runner-cli` Dockerfile stage installs four AI coding-agent CLIs globally with no version pins, meaning every image rebuild silently pulls whatever each package's `latest` tag currently resolves to, with no lockfile, checksum, or `--ignore-scripts` protection, for tools that get filesystem, shell, and (per the docker-socket finding filed alongside this one) Docker-daemon access.

## Evidence
- `Dockerfile:348`: `npm install -g --no-audit --no-fund @openai/codex @anthropic-ai/claude-code droid openclaw@latest` — no version specified for `@openai/codex`, `@anthropic-ai/claude-code`, or `droid`; `openclaw` explicitly pins to `@latest`.
- This `runner-cli` stage is the build target consumed by `docker-compose.yml`'s `omniroute-cli` service and by `docker-compose.prod.yml:53`, so it reaches a production-labeled compose file, not only a local dev convenience image.
- This install is outside the coverage of both Trivy (scans installed package versions at a point in time, not install-time integrity of a floating tag) and Socket's `projectIgnorePaths` configuration (doesn't cover ad hoc `npm install -g` calls inside a Dockerfile `RUN` step).

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/Dockerfile#L348

## Why this matters
An unpinned `npm install -g` in a Dockerfile means the exact code that ends up in every built image is decided by the npm registry at build time, not by anything reviewed or committed in this repository. Combined with the elevated access these specific tools already have in the `omniroute-cli` container (shell execution, Docker socket in some configurations), a compromised publish of any of the four packages reaches production images automatically on the next rebuild, with no diff for anyone to review.

## Attack or failure scenario
A supply-chain compromise of any of the four upstream packages (compromised maintainer account, malicious dependency-confusion publish, or a build-time postinstall script) ships in its next `latest`/unpinned release. The next `docker build` of the `runner-cli` stage — whether a scheduled rebuild, a release pipeline run, or a developer's local build — pulls the compromised version with no version-pin mismatch to flag it, and no lockfile diff for review to catch it before the image ships.

## Root cause
Global `npm install -g` inside a Dockerfile bypasses the project's own lockfile discipline (`package-lock.json` exists and is used for the app's own dependencies) entirely for these four packages.

## Recommended fix
Pin explicit versions for all four packages (`@openai/codex@X.Y.Z`, `@anthropic-ai/claude-code@X.Y.Z`, `droid@X.Y.Z`, `openclaw@X.Y.Z`) and update them via a deliberate, reviewed bump (ideally with the same Dependabot/Renovate-style process, if one exists, used for the rest of the dependency tree) rather than tracking `latest` implicitly on every rebuild.

## Acceptance criteria
- `Dockerfile:348` (or wherever this line moves to) specifies an exact version for each of the four packages.
- A documented process (or automation) exists for deliberately bumping these pins, rather than leaving them to float.

## Suggested labels
dependencies, docker

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — not independently exploitable without a compromised upstream package, but removes the last line of defense (pinning) against exactly that class of supply-chain attack for tools with elevated container access.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact Dockerfile line and traced which compose files/stages consume the `runner-cli` target.

body:
## Summary
`socket.yml` and the surrounding Socket.dev documentation (`SECURITY.md`, `docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md`) present what reads like an enforced supply-chain scanning pipeline, but no GitHub Actions workflow, `package.json` script, or `Makefile` target actually invokes Socket.dev — the config only shapes ignore-paths for Socket's own external, registry-side scan of the published npm package, and is not a gate on PRs, merges, or releases in this repository.

## Evidence
- `socket.yml` present at repo root, version 2, with a detailed `projectIgnorePaths` configuration.
- `grep -rn "socket" .github/workflows/*.yml package.json Makefile` (excluding unrelated matches like `net.Socket`/`websocket`) returns no reference to Socket.dev, `socketsecurity`, or any Socket CLI/action invocation.
- The maintainer stated directly on issue #7212 that Socket.dev integration is "out of scope... if you want to add Socket.dev scanning to your fork, the standard GitHub Action marketplace has Socket Security actions" — confirming this is a known, accepted gap rather than an oversight, but the surrounding documentation (`SECURITY.md`, `docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md`) does not make that limitation clear to a reader who encounters `socket.yml` and assumes it's wired into CI.
- Issue #2863 (a real Socket.dev finding that led to a v3.8.6 fix) confirms Socket *did* flag something real for this project — via its external, registry-side scan of the published package, not a repo-side gate.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/socket.yml

## Why this matters
A supply-chain-scanning config file that isn't wired into CI provides no protection against a malicious or compromised dependency landing in a PR before release — the only backstop is Socket's own external scan of the already-published npm package, which fires after the fact (as it did for #2863). Given this repository's explicit investment in supply-chain hygiene elsewhere (`.gitleaks.toml`, `.trivyignore`, `.zizmor.yml`), this is a gap in an otherwise deliberately hardened area, and the documentation's framing could give maintainers/contributors false confidence that dependency changes are being scanned pre-merge when they are not.

## Attack or failure scenario
A malicious dependency version (typosquat, compromised maintainer account, or a subtly backdoored transitive update) is introduced via a routine dependency-bump PR. Nothing in CI runs Socket.dev (or an equivalent) against the changed dependency tree before merge; the only chance of catching it is Socket's own after-the-fact scan of the next published release, or another tool (Trivy, gitleaks) catching an unrelated symptom.

## Root cause
`socket.yml`'s presence and the accompanying documentation imply an enforced pipeline that does not exist in this repository; the actual protection is an external, asynchronous, post-publish scan the maintainer has explicitly decided not to replicate as a repo-side CI gate.

## Recommended fix
Either wire a Socket Security GitHub Action (or equivalent open-source supply-chain scanner already compatible with this repo's stack — e.g. extending the existing `.trivyignore`/Trivy setup to cover dependency CVEs pre-merge) into a workflow that runs on dependency-changing PRs, or update `SECURITY.md`/`docs/security/SOCKET_DEV_FINDINGS.md` to state plainly that `socket.yml` governs only the external post-publish scan and is not a CI gate, so the documentation matches reality.

## Acceptance criteria
- Either a CI workflow demonstrably invokes dependency/supply-chain scanning gated on PR merge, or the security documentation is corrected to accurately describe `socket.yml`'s actual (external, post-publish, non-blocking) scope.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: documentation), documentation, dependencies

## Priority
P2

## Severity
Medium — no active exploit, but a real gap in pre-merge supply-chain defense and a documentation-vs-reality mismatch in a security-sensitive area.

## Confidence
Confirmed — maintainer's own statement on #7212 plus direct grep confirming no workflow invokes Socket.dev.

body:
## Summary
The `omniroute-cli` Docker Compose service (profile `cli`) bind-mounts the host's Docker socket (`/var/run/docker.sock`) into a container that also globally installs four unpinned (`latest`) AI coding-agent CLIs capable of executing arbitrary shell/tool commands, plus a read-write mount of the host repository. This combination is undocumented anywhere in the README or `docs/` tree and gives any command executed by one of those agents an effective path to root on the host via the Docker socket.

## Evidence
- `docker-compose.yml:158-177` (service `omniroute-cli`, profile `cli`):
  - `/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` (line ~173) — no comment explaining the risk, unlike the Redis bind-address comment nine lines above the equivalent section for that service.
  - `${AUTO_UPDATE_HOST_REPO_DIR:-.}:/workspace/omniroute:rw` (line ~175) — read-write host repo mount in the same container.
- `Dockerfile:348` (target `runner-cli`, the build target this service uses): `npm install -g --no-audit --no-fund @openai/codex @anthropic-ai/claude-code droid openclaw@latest` — four agent CLIs installed with no version pins.
- `grep -rn "docker.sock" README.md docs/` returns no results — this mount is not documented or flagged as a power-user/security tradeoff anywhere a user would see before enabling the `cli` profile.

Permalink (commit `7802f6e`): https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/blob/7802f6ea163f18f349348dbfd8710a159ac32e15/docker-compose.yml#L158-L177

## Why this matters
Docker socket access is equivalent to root on the host — any process that can talk to `/var/run/docker.sock` can start a privileged, host-network, host-filesystem-mounted container and fully escape. Placing that socket inside the same container as multiple general-purpose AI agent CLIs (whose entire purpose is executing commands on request, including from remote/untrusted instructions such as prompt-injected content in a fetched web page or file) turns any agent misbehavior or prompt injection into a full host compromise, not just a contained sandbox escape.

## Attack or failure scenario
An operator enables the `cli` profile so an AI agent can help manage their OmniRoute deployment. The agent is later given (directly or via prompt injection in content it reads, e.g. a webpage, email, or file it's asked to summarize) a command that creates a new Docker container with `-v /:/host --privileged`, mounting the entire host filesystem read-write into a new container the agent controls — a standard Docker-socket container-escape technique. Because none of the agent CLIs are pinned, a compromised or backdoored release of any of the four packages would have the same access without requiring any prompt injection at all.

## Root cause
No isolation between "give an AI agent shell access to help operate this service" and "give that same environment root-equivalent host access via the Docker socket." The mount was added without a corresponding trust-boundary comment or opt-in confirmation, unlike the project's own pattern for lower-stakes decisions (e.g. the Redis bind-address comment).

## Recommended fix
- Remove the Docker socket mount from `omniroute-cli` unless a specific, narrow feature requires it; if a feature does require Docker control, use a scoped Docker socket proxy (e.g. a `docker-socket-proxy` sidecar with an explicit allowlisted API subset) instead of the raw socket.
- If the raw socket must stay for now, add an explicit, prominent warning in the compose file (matching the Redis precedent) and in the README/docs section describing the `cli` profile, stating plainly that enabling it grants host-root-equivalent access to anything the contained agents execute.
- Pin the four agent CLI packages to specific versions in the Dockerfile and update them deliberately, rather than tracking `latest`.

## Acceptance criteria
- The `cli` profile either no longer mounts the raw Docker socket, or its documentation (compose comment + README/docs) explicitly states the host-root-equivalent risk before an operator opts in.
- Agent CLI versions in the `runner-cli` Dockerfile stage are pinned.

## Suggested labels
security (label does not exist on this repo — nearest available: bug), bug, docker

## Priority
P1

## Severity
High — requires the operator to have opted into the `cli` profile, but the risk is undocumented and the blast radius (host root) is severe.

## Confidence
Confirmed — verified the exact compose lines, the Dockerfile install command, and the absence of any documentation via direct grep across README.md and docs/.

title: fix(gamification): action_count badges are computed over a 30-day-pruned xp_audit_log
body:
### Problem / Use Case

The four `request` action-count badges are computed over a table that is pruned every 30 days by default, so the lifetime totals they describe can never be reached on a default install.

`checkActionCountBadges()` (`src/lib/gamification/events.ts:171-198`, called from `emitGamificationEvent` at `:104` on every awarded action) counts rows in `xp_audit_log`:

```ts
"SELECT COALESCE(COUNT(*), 0) AS count FROM xp_audit_log WHERE api_key_id = ? AND action = ?"
```

and compares the result with the thresholds `first-token` 1, `token-consumer` 1,000, `token-machine` 10,000, `token-whale` 100,000 (`events.ts:185-198`). `getActionCount()` in `src/lib/gamification/badges.ts:324-342` does the same for the `action_count` criteria that `evaluateBadges()` reads.

Since #6801 (PR #7260), `cleanupXpAuditLog()` (`src/lib/db/cleanup.ts:348-368`) deletes every `xp_audit_log` row older than `retention.xpAuditLog` days and runs inside `runAutoCleanup()` (`cleanup.ts:460`). The default is 30 days (`src/types/databaseSettings.ts:125`, schema cap 365 in `src/shared/validation/settingsSchemas.ts:573`) and auto-cleanup is on by default.

So with the defaults the badge descriptions in `badges.ts:32-59` ("Made 1,000 API requests", "Made 10,000 API requests", "Made 100,000 API requests") are effectively "made N requests inside the last 30 days". A key that sends 900 requests a month for a year never unlocks Token Consumer; Token Whale needs about 3,300 requests a day, every day. The `token_share` ladder (`generous` 1,000 up to `community-hero` 1,000,000) has the same shape, and the `unique_count` (`badges.ts:349-362`) and `first` (`badges.ts:485-501`, `MIN(created_at)`) criteria read the same pruned table.

**Reproduction** (focused test against `release/v3.8.51`, temp `DATA_DIR`, default retention):

1. Insert 1,200 `xp_audit_log` rows for one key, `action = 'request'`, `created_at = '2026-07-01 12:00:00'`.
2. The `events.ts:178` query returns 1200.
3. `await cleanupXpAuditLog()` returns `{ deleted: 1200 }`; the same query now returns 0.
4. `await emitGamificationEvent({ apiKeyId, action: "request" })` — the query returns 1, `hasBadge(key, "token-consumer")` is `false` although the key has made 1,201 requests.

```
{ before: 1200, deleted: 1200, after: 0 }
{ afterRequest: 1, tokenConsumer: false, firstToken: true }
```

The same sequence with rows dated inside the window unlocks the badge, which is what makes this a retention interaction and not a badge bug.

### Proposed Solution

Two ways to make the counts durable; the choice is yours:

**Option A — durable per-key, per-action counter (recommended).** Add a small `xp_action_counts (api_key_id, action, count, updated_at)` table incremented in `addXp()` (`src/lib/db/gamification.ts:157-174`, the single insert point) in the same statement batch as the audit row, backfilled once from whatever `xp_audit_log` still holds in the migration, and read by both `checkActionCountBadges()` and `getActionCount()`. Retention keeps pruning the audit log; badges no longer depend on it. This mirrors how `user_levels.total_xp` already survives the prune.

**Option B — exclude `xp_audit_log` from the default prune.** Set the default to the 365-day cap or make the row opt-in, and add a note to the retention setting that pruning resets the request badges. Cheapest change, but it only stretches the window and gives back the unbounded growth #6801 wanted to stop.

Either way the badge descriptions and the retention setting's help text should agree on what is being counted.

### Alternatives Considered

- Counting from `call_logs` / usage history instead of the audit log: those tables have their own retention (`callLogs`, `usageHistory` in the same settings block) and are not keyed by gamification action, so the same problem moves rather than disappears.
- Using `user_levels.total_xp / XP per request` as a proxy: XP per action is not constant (anti-cheat can reject awards, `token_share` and `daily_login` add XP) so the derived count drifts.
- Pinning the count on the first row's `id` (`MAX(id) - MIN(id)`): breaks as soon as several keys interleave.

### Acceptance Criteria

- With default retention, a key whose `request` rows are older than 30 days still unlocks `token-consumer` on its 1,000th lifetime request after cleanup has run.
- `cleanupXpAuditLog()` keeps deleting audit rows; `runAutoCleanup()` result shape is unchanged.
- `getActionCount()` and `checkActionCountBadges()` agree on the same source.
- Existing `tests/unit/db-cleanup-xp-audit-log.test.ts` and `tests/unit/gamification/*` stay green.

### Area

Analytics / Usage Tracking, Other (gamification)

### Related Provider(s)

None

### Additional Context

Retention prune introduced by #6801 / #7260. Badge dedup guard: #3472. Sibling gamification issue on the same award path: #12426. Base `release/v3.8.51`, commit `1a0375f`.

### Expected Test Plan

- New unit test that seeds rows outside the window, runs `cleanupXpAuditLog()`, emits one `request` event and asserts the badge unlocks (red on the current base, green with either option).
- Migration test for the backfill if Option A is chosen.
- `tests/unit/db-cleanup-xp-audit-log.test.ts`, `tests/unit/gamification/*.test.ts`, `typecheck:core`, `check:db-rules`.

I can send a PR demonstrating whichever option you prefer.

title: fix(images): /v1/images/edits flattens a combo to its first target and never falls back
body:
### Problem / Use Case `/v1/images/edits` accepts a combo name, but it flattens the combo to its first target and never tries the others, while `/v1/images/generations` runs the full combo strategy with per-target fallback since #9239. The same combo therefore behaves differently on the two image routes. Where it happens on `release/v3.8.51`: - `resolveSingleImageComboTarget()` (`src/lib/images/imageRouteModel.ts:60-75`) returns only the first target that has a `modelStr`; `resolveImageRouteModel()` uses it for every bare (slash-less) name at `:91-96`. - `src/app/api/v1/images/edits/route.ts:346-365` calls `resolveImageRouteModel(fullModel)` once and continues with a single `resolvedModel`. There is no `getComboByName` / `executeImageCombo` diversion in that file; the one in `generations/route.ts:155-163` runs *before* `resolveImageRouteModel` precisely "so we skip single-target flattening" (comment at `:156`). - The edit-capable branches are `codex-responses` (`edits/route.ts:395`), `fal-ai` edit models (`:484`), `adobe-firefly-image` (`:532`), `openrouter` (`:551`) and custom OpenAI-compatible nodes (`:605+`). Anything else with a built-in config gets `400 Image edit is not supported for built-in provider "

"` at `:597-603`; a built-in with no credentials gets `401 No credentials for provider` at `:414-419`; a custom node with none gets `400` at `:623-628`; rate limits return `429` at `:420` / `:629`. Concrete case — combo `img-edit` with targets `[openai/gpt-image-2, codex/gpt-image-2]` or `[adobe-firefly/firefly-image-4, codex/gpt-image-2]`, Codex credentials present: - `POST /v1/images/generations {"model":"img-edit"}` → `executeImageCombo` filters image-capable targets, iterates them, skips the ones without credentials or rate-limited (`open-sse/services/imageCombo.ts:98-122`), returns the first success with `fallbackAttempts` in the meta headers. - `POST /v1/images/edits` with `model=img-edit` → resolves to the first target and answers `400 Image edit is not supported for built-in provider "openai"` (or `401 No credentials for provider: adobe-firefly` when Firefly is first and not connected). The second target could have served the edit and is never consulted. The combo's order also matters more than it should: a user who lists a generation-only provider first gets a hard 400 on edits even though the combo is perfectly valid for generations. ### Proposed Solution Give `/v1/images/edits` the same combo semantics as generations, in two steps so the first is a pure refactor: 1. Extract the target loop of `executeImageCombo()` (`imageCombo.ts:83-156`: credential resolution, `allRateLimited` skip, terminal-vs-retryable classification, fallback count) into a generic `runImageComboTargets(targets, { filter, dispatch })` and have `executeImageCombo` call it with `handleImageGeneration` as the dispatch. No behaviour change on generations. 2. In `edits/route.ts`, when the model is a bare combo name, run the same loop with an edit-capable filter (Codex, Firefly, Fal edit models, OpenRouter, custom OpenAI-compatible nodes) and a dispatch that reuses the route's existing per-provider branches; keep the terminal statuses (400/401/403) terminal per target so a combo with no edit-capable target still answers clearly, and surface `fallbackAttempts` in the meta headers as generations does. Open points I would like your call on before writing it: - Whether a target that answers 401 (no credentials) should be skipped like on generations (`imageCombo.ts:109-113` treats missing credentials as retryable) or stay terminal as the edits route does today. - Whether the combo diversion should also apply to `n > 1` / multi-reference requests, or only to the single-image path first. ### Alternatives Considered - Only re-ordering the combo in the dashboard: works for one user, but any combo that mixes generation-only and edit-capable providers stays order-sensitive on edits and not on generations. - Making `resolveSingleImageComboTarget` prefer an edit-capable target when called from the edits route: fixes the 400 but still gives up on the first credential/rate-limit failure, so it is half of the generations behaviour. - Having the edits route call `executeImageCombo` directly: not possible today, it dispatches `handleImageGeneration` and does not carry the multipart image bytes, hence the generic runner in step 1. ### Acceptance Criteria - `POST /v1/images/edits` with a bare combo name whose first target is not edit-capable, and whose later target is, returns the later target's result with `fallbackAttempts >= 1`. - A combo with no edit-capable target returns one 400 that names the combo, not the first provider. - Rate-limited (429) and 5xx targets fall through to the next target; the last error is returned when all fail, as on generations. - `/v1/images/generations` combo behaviour and `tests/unit/combo/image-combo.test.ts` are unchanged by step 1. ### Area Proxy / Routing, Provider Support ### Related Provider(s) Codex, Adobe Firefly, Fal, OpenRouter, OpenAI-compatible custom providers ### Additional Context Combo/alias resolution on both routes: #3214 / #3215 (PR #3219), bare combos over aliases: #3527. Full combo strategy on generations only: #9239 (PR #9499; `open-sse/services/imageCombo.ts`, `src/app/api/v1/images/generations/route.ts`). Response shape fix that touched both routes: #12268 / PR #12362. Base `release/v3.8.51`, commit `1a0375f`. ### Expected Test Plan - Extend `tests/unit/image-routes-combo-edits-3214-3215.test.ts` (the file #9239's test plan pointed at for multi-target combos) with: first target generation-only + second Codex → 200 from Codex; first target without credentials + second with → 200; no edit-capable target → single 400; all rate-limited → 429. - Keep `tests/unit/combo/image-combo.test.ts` green after the extraction, plus `image-generation-route`, `8510-adobe-firefly-edits-route`, `10197-openrouter-image-edits-route`, `fal-image-edit`; `typecheck:core`, `check:open-sse-typecheck`, `check-complexity-ratchets`. Happy to send the two PRs (refactor first, then the edits wiring) once you have picked the 401 semantics.

body:
## What

`docker-publish` on `release/v3.8.51` is red since 2026-08-30 01:32Z (run [33279620488](https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/actions/runs/33279620488)): the blocking **Trivy CRITICAL gate** now reports

| Library | Vulnerability | Installed | Fixed | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go `stdlib` | [CVE-2025-68121](https://avd.aquasec.com/nvd/cve-2025-68121) — `crypto/tls`: incorrect certificate validation during TLS session resumption | v1.24.1 | 1.24.13 / 1.25.7 | `app/node_modules/tls-client-node/bin/tls-client-linux-ubuntu-amd64-1.15.1.so` (gobinary) |

Nothing in the repo changed — the CVE entered Trivy's DB (the 08-29 18:43Z build on `main` skips the gate; the gate runs for every non-`main` image, so it also blocks the **`v3.8.51` tag build**).

## Why there is no bump

- The `.so` is fetched by `tls-client-node`'s postinstall from the **latest GitHub release of `bogdanfinn/tls-client`** — `v1.15.1` (2026-06-08) is still the latest and its `go.mod` declares `go 1.24.1`. No rebuilt upstream binary exists.
- `tls-client-node` npm: `0.2.0` is `latest` (2026-06-03); `1.0.4` is an older, different package lineage (April), not a fix.
- `ignore-unfixed: true` does not cover it because Go **has** a fixed stdlib version — only the upstream binary is not rebuilt.

## Remedy applied (per `docs/security/SUPPLY_CHAIN.md` → "CVE Variance", item 2)

`.trivyignore` entry for `CVE-2025-68121` with justification + this issue as tracker + expiry. Exposure note: the binary is only loaded by the web-provider executors that impersonate a browser TLS fingerprint (claude-web / grok-web / lmarena / perplexity-web / notion-web); handshakes go through `bogdanfinn/utls`, and the affected path is `crypto/tls` session resumption on the client side.

## To close this issue

Any of: a `bogdanfinn/tls-client` release built with Go ≥ 1.24.13 (then remove the `.trivyignore` line and verify the gate); or build the `.so` ourselves from `v1.15.1` sources with a patched Go toolchain and pin it via `TLS_CLIENT_VERSION` / a vendored asset. Revisit at the next base-image / dep bump and **before the `v3.8.51` tag**.

Parent: #9760

Target branch: release/v3.8.51. Do not merge into frozen release/v3.8.50.

Problem
Historical Video Bridge plans, backlog snapshots, comparisons, ledgers, and current docs contain conflicting completion claims. Final closure needs one current authority tied to merged SHAs and exact environment receipts.

Scope
- Update public guardrail and release documentation to describe only verified behavior.
- Establish one private CURRENT ledger with implementation_state, verification_evidence, and promotion_evidence for VB-FU-01 through VB-FU-09.
- Mark older private artifacts historical or superseded without deleting or rewriting history.
- Reconcile original and canonical post-merge SHAs.
- Persist the complete VPS 192.168.0.15 matrix, live smokes, CI attribution, build, pack, boot, UI, FFmpeg, STT, and eval receipts.
- Produce a final handoff and a separate postmortem covering the earlier false 9 of 9 closure.

Acceptance
- Public docs pass check:docs-all and contain no fabricated paths, endpoints, settings, commands, or mutable counts.
- CURRENT has no contradictory complete, partial, HOLD, or not_applicable state.
- Every implementation PR is merged and ancestral to release/v3.8.51.
- Exact merged SHA passes the required VPS and CI matrix.
- No required check is red, stale, cancelled, skipped, or unattributed.
- Test settings and temporary VPS artifacts are restored and cleanup is recorded.
- The feature is called 100 percent complete only when every gate in the approved closure plan is satisfied.
